acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Cannabis withdrawal is a recognized syndrome in the DSM-5. About half of people who use cannabis regularly experience symptoms like irritability, anxiety, poor sleep, and reduced appetite when they stop.

mainEntity.name: How long does cannabis withdrawal last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Symptoms usually begin within one to three days, peak between days two and six, and ease over about two weeks. Sleep problems and low mood can linger for four to six weeks.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common cannabis withdrawal symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most reported symptoms are irritability, anxiety, trouble sleeping, vivid dreams, reduced appetite, restlessness, and low mood. Headaches, sweating, chills, and stomach discomfort can also appear.

For most people it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. Unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, it does not typically cause seizures. Seek help if low mood becomes severe or you have thoughts of self-harm.

mainEntity.name: Do I need medical detox to quit cannabis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most people can quit cannabis at home without medical detox. A supervised program can help if you use very heavily, have a mental health condition, or have relapsed before.

mainEntity.name: Is there a medication for cannabis use disorder?

acceptedAnswer.text: No medication is approved in Canada or the United States specifically for cannabis use disorder. The treatments with the strongest evidence are behavioural therapies like CBT and motivational enhancement therapy.

mainEntity.name: Can you get addicted to cannabis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Roughly one in ten adults who use cannabis will develop cannabis use disorder, and the risk is higher for those who start young or use daily.

mainEntity.name: Why can't I sleep after quitting cannabis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cannabis suppresses REM sleep. When you stop, REM rebounds, bringing vivid dreams and restless nights. Sleep usually normalizes within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Why can’t I sleep after quitting cannabis?

answer_blocks.text: Cannabis suppresses REM sleep. When you stop, REM rebounds, which brings vivid dreams and restless nights. If you had been using cannabis to fall asleep, your body also has to relearn how to do it without help. Sleep usually normalizes within a few weeks.

faqs.question: What is cannabis use disorder?

answer_blocks.text: Cannabis use disorder is the clinical term for continued cannabis use that causes harm and becomes hard to control. The DSM-5 grades it as mild, moderate, or severe based on how many of eleven criteria a person meets over a year, such as cravings, tolerance, and failed attempts to cut down.

faqs.question: How much cannabis use leads to withdrawal?

faqs.question: Does quitting cannabis cause depression?

answer_blocks.text: Cravings tend to be strongest in the first two weeks and fade over time. Distraction, exercise, avoiding triggers, staying connected to supportive people, and having a written plan for high-risk moments all help. Counselling teaches specific skills to ride cravings out.

answer_blocks.text: Yes. Reduced appetite and mild weight loss are common in the first week or two of withdrawal. Appetite returns to normal as your body adjusts, usually within a couple of weeks.

blocks.html: Cannabis Withdrawal Is Real: Symptoms, Timeline, and How to Quit Safely in Canada

blocks.text: Plenty of people are told that cannabis is not addictive and that quitting is easy. Then they try to stop after months or years of daily use, and the first week hits them harder than they expected. Sleep falls apart. They feel irritable, anxious, and off their food. Some start to wonder if something is wrong with them.
blocks.html: Plenty of people are told that cannabis is not addictive and that quitting is easy. Then they try to stop after months or years of daily use, and the first week hits them harder than they expected. Sleep falls apart. They feel irritable, anxious, and off their food. Some start to wonder if something is wrong with them.

blocks.text: Nothing is wrong with them. What they are feeling has a name. Cannabis withdrawal is a recognized medical syndrome, and it affects a large share of people who use regularly. It is rarely dangerous the way alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal can be, but it is real, it is uncomfortable, and it is one of the main reasons people give up and go back to using before their body has a chance to reset.

blocks.text: This guide walks through what cannabis withdrawal actually feels like, how long each stage lasts, why sleep and mood are the slowest to recover, and what genuinely helps. It is written for Canadians, so the statistics, treatment options, and support services all reflect what is available here.

blocks.text: The short answer
blocks.html: The short answer

blocks.text: Cannabis withdrawal happens when someone who has been using cannabis heavily and regularly cuts back or stops. Symptoms usually begin within one to three days, peak around days two to six, and fade over about two weeks. Sleep problems and low mood can linger for a month or longer. Roughly half of people who use cannabis frequently will notice withdrawal when they quit. It is treatable, and the discomfort is temporary.

blocks.text: Is cannabis withdrawal actually real?
blocks.html: Is cannabis withdrawal actually real?

blocks.text: Yes. For years the common belief was that cannabis could not cause physical dependence. Research has settled that question. The condition is formally listed as cannabis withdrawal in the DSM-5, the diagnostic manual that Canadian and American clinicians use, and it sits alongside cannabis use disorder as a documented consequence of heavy use.
blocks.html: Yes. For years the common belief was that cannabis could not cause physical dependence. Research has settled that question. The condition is formally listed as cannabis withdrawal in the DSM-5, the diagnostic manual that Canadian and American clinicians use, and it sits alongside cannabis use disorder as a documented consequence of heavy use.

blocks.text: The reason it took so long to be recognized is that cannabis leaves the body slowly. THC is stored in fat and releases gradually, so withdrawal comes on later and more gently than it does with a short-acting drug. That slow taper is also why the symptoms can drag on for weeks rather than clearing in a few days. A 2020 review published in the journal JAMA Network Open found that close to half of regular, dependent cannabis users experience a withdrawal syndrome when they stop, which lines up with what clinicians see every day.

blocks.text: Recognizing withdrawal as real matters because people who do not expect it often blame themselves. They think the anxiety and insomnia mean they are broken, when it is simply their brain adjusting to life without a substance it had come to rely on. If you have noticed the warning signs of a growing marijuana problem, withdrawal is often the clearest confirmation that dependence has taken hold.

blocks.html: What cannabis withdrawal feels like

blocks.text: Cannabis withdrawal is mostly psychological and emotional, with a handful of physical symptoms mixed in. The DSM-5 lists a specific cluster, and a diagnosis generally requires at least three of them appearing within a week of cutting back. Here is what people typically report.

blocks.text: For most people the standout complaints are irritability, anxiety, and wrecked sleep. Those three do the most damage to daily life, and they are the symptoms most likely to push someone back toward using just to feel normal again. The physical symptoms are usually milder, though the headaches and appetite loss can be genuinely unpleasant in the first several days.

blocks.text: The cannabis withdrawal timeline, day by day
blocks.html: The cannabis withdrawal timeline, day by day

blocks.text: Withdrawal follows a fairly predictable arc, although the exact timing shifts from person to person depending on how much and how long they used. The table below shows the general pattern.

blocks.text: Stage Timing What usually happens Onset Day 1 to 3 Irritability, anxiety, appetite loss, and trouble sleeping begin as THC levels fall. Peak Day 2 to 6 Symptoms are at their strongest. Mood swings, insomnia, headaches, sweating, and cravings are most intense. Early easing Day 7 to 14 Physical symptoms fade. Appetite returns. Mood and sleep start to improve but stay unsteady. blocks.text: The most important thing to understand about this timeline is that the worst part is short. The peak lasts only a few days. If you can get past that first week, the acute discomfort is largely behind you. This is the same pattern that shows up across other drugs, and if you have read about the cocaine withdrawal timeline or the meth withdrawal experience, you will notice that the sharpest phase is always early, followed by a longer stretch of mood and sleep recovery.

blocks.text: Why sleep and mood take the longest to heal
blocks.html: Why sleep and mood take the longest to heal

blocks.text: Ask anyone who has quit heavy cannabis use what the hardest part was, and most will say the sleep. Cannabis suppresses REM sleep, the dreaming stage. When you stop, REM comes flooding back, which is why so many people report strange, intense, sometimes exhausting dreams in the first few weeks. On top of that, falling asleep without cannabis can feel impossible for someone who had been using it as a nightly sleep aid.

blocks.text: Mood follows a similar slow curve. The brain’s own cannabinoid system had been dialing itself down to compensate for a steady outside supply. It takes time to recalibrate, and during that stretch people often feel flat, anxious, or unusually reactive. This lingering phase is sometimes described as a form of post-acute withdrawal, and it is the same principle behind the drawn-out recovery seen after benzodiazepine withdrawal and heavy alcohol use.

blocks.text: Severity Criteria met What it often looks like Mild 2 to 3 Using more than intended, some failed attempts to cut down, early impact on daily life. Moderate 4 to 5 Cravings, neglected responsibilities, giving up activities, continued use despite problems. Severe 6 or more Tolerance, withdrawal, large amounts of time spent using or recovering, use despite clear harm.

blocks.text: The eleven criteria cover things like tolerance, withdrawal, unsuccessful attempts to quit, cravings, and continuing to use even when it is hurting your relationships, work, or health. You do not need to hit rock bottom to qualify, and you do not need to wait until things are severe to get help. Many people benefit from support at the mild or moderate stage, which is often when change is easiest. If you are unsure where you land, reading through how marijuana addiction develops can help you see the pattern more clearly.

blocks.text: Cannabis in Canada: what the numbers show
blocks.html: Cannabis in Canada: what the numbers show

blocks.text: Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, and the country now has some of the most detailed cannabis data in the world through the annual Canadian Cannabis Survey run by Health Canada. The picture it paints is worth knowing.

blocks.text: Two numbers stand out. First, about a quarter of people who use cannabis do so daily or almost daily, and daily use is the pattern most likely to lead to dependence and withdrawal. Second, cannabis use among younger Canadians is high, which matters because the developing brain is more vulnerable to lasting effects. That is part of why substance use among youth in Canadian schools remains a focus for parents, educators, and clinicians.

blocks.text: Legalization did not create a wave of new dependence, but it did make cannabis more available and more potent. Today’s products often contain far more THC than the cannabis of past decades, and higher potency tends to mean stronger withdrawal for heavy users.

blocks.text: How to get through cannabis withdrawal safely
blocks.html: How to get through cannabis withdrawal safely

blocks.text: Most people can manage cannabis withdrawal at home. It does not usually require medical detox the way alcohol or opioids might. Still, a few practical steps make a real difference in that first difficult week.
blocks.html: Most people can manage cannabis withdrawal at home. It does not usually require medical detox the way alcohol or opioids might. Still, a few practical steps make a real difference in that first difficult week.

blocks.text: Hydrate and eat regularly, even when your appetite is low. Move your body a little each day, since light exercise helps with both mood and sleep. Protect your sleep routine by cutting caffeine in the afternoon, keeping screens out of bed, and going to sleep at the same time each night. Lean on people who support your decision, and plan ahead for the moments and places that usually trigger you to use.

blocks.text: There is one important safety note. If your low mood becomes severe, if you feel hopeless, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself, treat that as a reason to reach out for help right away rather than something to push through alone. Withdrawal can unmask or worsen depression and anxiety, and those deserve proper care. A dual diagnosis approach that treats mental health and substance use together tends to work far better than tackling either one on its own.

blocks.text: For people with very heavy use, a mental health condition, or a history of relapse, starting in a supervised setting can be the safer choice. A structured detox program gives you monitoring, sleep support, and a calm environment away from your usual triggers. Options range from medically supervised detox to gentler community-based drug detox services, depending on what you need.

blocks.text: Counselling is the heart of cannabis use disorder treatment, since there is no approved medication for it.

blocks.text: Treatment that actually works for cannabis use disorder
blocks.html: Treatment that actually works for cannabis use disorder

blocks.text: Here is something that surprises a lot of people. There is no medication approved in Canada or the United States specifically for cannabis use disorder. Researchers have tested THC substitutes, cannabidiol, gabapentin, and several antidepressants, with modest and inconsistent results. That means the treatments with the strongest evidence are all behavioural. The good news is that they work.

blocks.text: Approach How it helps Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) Identifies the triggers and thought patterns behind use and builds practical coping skills. Motivational enhancement therapy Strengthens your own reasons for change and resolves the mixed feelings that stall progress. Contingency management Uses concrete rewards for drug-free test results to reinforce early abstinence. Family and group therapy Rebuilds support at home and connects you with others who understand the struggle.

Talk therapy like cognitive and dialectical behavioural therapy gives you tools you keep for life, and many people find that one-on-one counselling is where the real work happens.

blocks.text: Choosing the right level of care
blocks.html: Choosing the right level of care

blocks.text: Cannabis use disorder can be treated at different intensities, and the right fit depends on how severe things are, whether other substances or mental health conditions are involved, and how stable your home life is.
blocks.html: Cannabis use disorder can be treated at different intensities, and the right fit depends on how severe things are, whether other substances or mental health conditions are involved, and how stable your home life is.

blocks.text: Level of care Best suited for Outpatient counselling Mild to moderate use disorder, a stable home, and the ability to keep up work or school. Intensive outpatient People who need several structured sessions a week but can still live at home. Residential or inpatient rehab Severe use, repeated relapse, co-occurring conditions, or a chaotic home environment.

blocks.text: Helping a loved one quit cannabis
blocks.html: Helping a loved one quit cannabis

blocks.text: If you are worried about someone else, the hardest part is often that cannabis feels harmless to them. They may point out that it is legal, that everyone they know uses it, and that they can stop whenever they want. Arguing about whether cannabis is dangerous rarely helps. What works better is staying curious and concerned rather than accusatory, and noticing out loud the specific ways it seems to be affecting their life.

blocks.text: Offer to help them find support rather than issuing ultimatums. Learn what withdrawal looks like so you are not alarmed when the first week is rough. And take care of your own wellbeing too, because supporting someone through change is draining. If the situation feels stuck, family therapy can open up conversations that keep hitting a wall at home, and our guidance on addiction in teens is a useful starting point if the person you are worried about is young.

blocks.text: Frequently asked questions about cannabis withdrawal
blocks.html: Frequently asked questions about cannabis withdrawal

blocks.text: Is cannabis withdrawal real?
blocks.html: Is cannabis withdrawal real?

blocks.text: Yes. Cannabis withdrawal is a recognized syndrome in the DSM-5. About half of people who use cannabis regularly experience symptoms like irritability, anxiety, poor sleep, and reduced appetite when they stop. It is real, and it is not a sign of weakness.
blocks.html: Yes. Cannabis withdrawal is a recognized syndrome in the DSM-5. About half of people who use cannabis regularly experience symptoms like irritability, anxiety, poor sleep, and reduced appetite when they stop. It is real, and it is not a sign of weakness.

blocks.text: How long does cannabis withdrawal last?
blocks.html: How long does cannabis withdrawal last?

blocks.text: Symptoms usually begin within one to three days, peak between days two and six, and ease over about two weeks. Sleep problems and low mood can linger for four to six weeks. The most intense phase is short, generally just a few days.
blocks.html: Symptoms usually begin within one to three days, peak between days two and six, and ease over about two weeks. Sleep problems and low mood can linger for four to six weeks. The most intense phase is short, generally just a few days.

blocks.text: What are the most common cannabis withdrawal symptoms?
blocks.html: What are the most common cannabis withdrawal symptoms?

blocks.text: The most reported symptoms are irritability, anxiety, trouble sleeping, vivid dreams, reduced appetite, restlessness, and low mood. Physical symptoms such as headaches, sweating, chills, and stomach discomfort can also appear, usually more mildly.
blocks.html: The most reported symptoms are irritability, anxiety, trouble sleeping, vivid dreams, reduced appetite, restlessness, and low mood. Physical symptoms such as headaches, sweating, chills, and stomach discomfort can also appear, usually more mildly.

blocks.text: Is cannabis withdrawal dangerous?
blocks.html: Is cannabis withdrawal dangerous?

blocks.text: For most people it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. Unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, it does not typically cause seizures or life-threatening complications. The main risk is that low mood or anxiety worsens, so seek help if you feel hopeless or have thoughts of self-harm.
blocks.html: For most people it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. Unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, it does not typically cause seizures or life-threatening complications. The main risk is that low mood or anxiety worsens, so seek help if you feel hopeless or have thoughts of self-harm.

blocks.text: Why can’t I sleep after quitting cannabis?
blocks.html: Why can’t I sleep after quitting cannabis?

blocks.text: Cannabis suppresses REM sleep. When you stop, REM rebounds, which brings vivid dreams and restless nights. If you had been using cannabis to fall asleep, your body also has to relearn how to do it without help. Sleep usually normalizes within a few weeks.

blocks.text: Do I need medical detox to quit cannabis?
blocks.html: Do I need medical detox to quit cannabis?

blocks.text: Most people can quit cannabis at home without medical detox. A supervised program can still help if you use very heavily, have a mental health condition, or have relapsed before, mainly for sleep support, monitoring, and a trigger-free environment.

blocks.text: What is cannabis use disorder?
blocks.html: What is cannabis use disorder?

blocks.text: Cannabis use disorder is the clinical term for continued cannabis use that causes harm and becomes hard to control. The DSM-5 grades it as mild, moderate, or severe based on how many of eleven criteria a person meets over a year, such as cravings, tolerance, and failed attempts to cut down.

The DSM-5 grades it as mild, moderate, or severe based on how many of eleven criteria a person meets over a year, such as cravings, tolerance, and failed attempts to cut down.

blocks.text: Is there a medication for cannabis withdrawal or addiction?
blocks.html: Is there a medication for cannabis withdrawal or addiction?

blocks.text: No medication is approved in Canada or the United States specifically for cannabis use disorder. Doctors sometimes use short-term aids for sleep or anxiety, but the treatments with the strongest evidence are behavioural therapies like CBT and motivational enhancement therapy.
blocks.html: No medication is approved in Canada or the United States specifically for cannabis use disorder. Doctors sometimes use short-term aids for sleep or anxiety, but the treatments with the strongest evidence are behavioural therapies like CBT and motivational enhancement therapy.

blocks.text: Can you get addicted to cannabis?
blocks.html: Can you get addicted to cannabis?

blocks.text: Yes. Research suggests roughly one in ten adults who use cannabis will develop cannabis use disorder, and the risk is higher for those who start young or use daily. Legal does not mean risk free, and daily use is the pattern most linked to dependence.
blocks.html: Yes. Research suggests roughly one in ten adults who use cannabis will develop cannabis use disorder, and the risk is higher for those who start young or use daily. Legal does not mean risk free, and daily use is the pattern most linked to dependence.

blocks.text: How much cannabis use leads to withdrawal?
blocks.html: How much cannabis use leads to withdrawal?

blocks.text: Withdrawal is most common in people who use daily or near daily over an extended period. Occasional users rarely notice it. Higher-potency products and concentrates increase the odds and the intensity of withdrawal symptoms.
blocks.html: Withdrawal is most common in people who use daily or near daily over an extended period. Occasional users rarely notice it. Higher-potency products and concentrates increase the odds and the intensity of withdrawal symptoms.

blocks.text: Does quitting cannabis cause depression?
blocks.html: Does quitting cannabis cause depression?

blocks.text: Low mood is a normal part of withdrawal as the brain readjusts, and it usually lifts within a few weeks. If depression is severe, lasts longer, or existed before you quit, it needs its own treatment, ideally alongside your substance use care.

blocks.text: What helps with cannabis cravings?
blocks.html: What helps with cannabis cravings?

blocks.text: Cravings tend to be strongest in the first two weeks and fade over time. Distraction, exercise, avoiding triggers, staying connected to supportive people, and having a written plan for high-risk moments all help. Counselling teaches specific skills to ride cravings out.
blocks.html: Cravings tend to be strongest in the first two weeks and fade over time. Distraction, exercise, avoiding triggers, staying connected to supportive people, and having a written plan for high-risk moments all help. Counselling teaches specific skills to ride cravings out.

blocks.text: Will my appetite come back after I stop using cannabis?
blocks.html: Will my appetite come back after I stop using cannabis?

blocks.text: Yes. Reduced appetite and mild weight loss are common in the first week or two of withdrawal. Appetite returns to normal as your body adjusts, usually within a couple of weeks.
blocks.html: Yes. Reduced appetite and mild weight loss are common in the first week or two of withdrawal. Appetite returns to normal as your body adjusts, usually within a couple of weeks.

blocks.text: Is cannabis withdrawal worse with edibles or concentrates?
blocks.html: Is cannabis withdrawal worse with edibles or concentrates?

blocks.text: Higher-THC products, including concentrates and frequent dabbing, deliver more THC and tend to produce stronger dependence, which can mean more intense withdrawal. The amount and frequency of use matter more than the specific form.
blocks.html: Higher-THC products, including concentrates and frequent dabbing, deliver more THC and tend to produce stronger dependence, which can mean more intense withdrawal. The amount and frequency of use matter more than the specific form.

blocks.text: Can teenagers experience cannabis withdrawal?
blocks.html: Can teenagers experience cannabis withdrawal?

blocks.text: Yes. Teens who use cannabis frequently can develop dependence and withdrawal, and the developing brain is more vulnerable to lasting effects. Early support makes a real difference, so it is worth acting sooner rather than later.
blocks.html: Yes. Teens who use cannabis frequently can develop dependence and withdrawal, and the developing brain is more vulnerable to lasting effects. Early support makes a real difference, so it is worth acting sooner rather than later.

blocks.text: How do I help someone who won’t admit their cannabis use is a problem?
blocks.html: How do I help someone who won’t admit their cannabis use is a problem?

blocks.text: Stay calm and specific, focus on the effects you have noticed rather than labels, and offer to help them find support instead of demanding they quit. Family therapy and a professional assessment can help when conversations at home keep stalling.

blocks.text: A final word
blocks.html: A final word

blocks.text: Cannabis withdrawal is real, but it is also temporary and manageable. The hardest days pass quickly, and the lingering sleep and mood changes fade with time. If cannabis has taken a bigger place in your life than you want, that is reason enough to reach out. Help is available, it works, and the first conversation is always free and confidential.
